# Four Positions on Open-Source AI Governance

---

## 1. Completely Open

**Steelman:**
The open-source movement has consistently proven that transparency accelerates both innovation and security. When code is publicly available, security researchers can identify vulnerabilities that closed systems hide. The "many eyes" hypothesis—that given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow—has driven internet infrastructure, cryptography, and software development for decades. Restricting open-source AI would concentrate power among a handful of corporations and states, creating a dangerous dependency on unaccountable gatekeepers. Moreover, the benefits of AI—medical diagnosis, climate modeling, educational tools—disproportionately serve the global south and under-resourced institutions when freely available. The internet's foundational architecture assumed openness; attempting to close Pandora's box after the fact is both futile and counterproductive.

**Typical Counter-Argument:**
AI differs categorically from traditional software because it can exhibit emergent capabilities and enable mass harm with minimal additional engineering. A model that helps write poetry can, with minimal fine-tuning, help synthesize dangerous knowledge. Unlike a vulnerability in a web server, a powerful AI model cannot be "patched" once released. The asymmetry between creation and destruction means that openness creates irreversible capabilities in the world—there's no way to un-know a technique once published.
